tip: The modal 'können' pairs with an infinitive parked at the very end: in 'Können Sie bitte langsamer sprechen?' the modal leads and 'sprechen' closes the clause.
'Herein' adds motion toward the speaker: 'hereinkommen' = to come in, toward me. 'Her' normally points to the speaker.
'Zu' always takes the dative, and 'zu' plus 'der' contracts to 'zur': 'zur Schule' = to school.
Many strong verbs shift 'a' to 'ä' in the 'du' and 'er' forms: 'fahren' becomes 'er fährt'.
'Danken' uses 'für' for what you thank someone for: 'danken für Ihre Hilfe', not 'danken über'.
English drops the to, but German marks it with dative: 'dem Mann etwas Geld' means some money to the man, shown by 'dem', not a preposition.
Time you spend takes the accusative with no preposition: 'den ganzen Nachmittag' = for the whole afternoon.
Genitive shows possession: 'die Geschichte dieses Landes' = the history of this country. Masculine and neuter nouns often add '-es', as in 'Landes'.
'Helfen' takes a dative object, so it is 'helfe meinem Vater', not 'den Vater'. English treats help as a direct-object verb, but German does not.
'Empfehlen' shifts 'e' to 'ie' in the 'du' and 'er' forms: 'sie empfiehlt', like 'sehen' and 'lesen'.
'Begegnen' takes the dative, and dative plural nouns normally add '-n': 'wir begegnen alten Freunden'.
'Eigen' means one's own and still needs a possessive and adjective ending: 'sein eigenes Geschäft' = his own business.
'Sich etwas anschauen' takes a dative reflexive: 'ich schaue mir ... einen Dokumentarfilm an' = I watch a documentary for myself.
'Sein' builds its own perfect with 'sein', not 'haben': 'wir sind ... gewesen' = we have been.
'Trotz' means despite and takes the genitive: 'trotz ihrer Erkältung' = despite her cold.
Any infinitive can become a capitalized neuter noun: 'kochen' becomes 'das Kochen', so 'vor dem Kochen' = before cooking.
'Darfst ... nicht' means must not, a ban: 'darfst ... nicht rauchen' = smoking is forbidden. Do not mix it with 'muss nicht', which means need not.
The idiom 'einen Blick werfen auf' means to take a look at; here 'werfe' means cast, not literally throw.
'Viertel vor sechs' = quarter to six, literally a quarter before six. 'Vor' counts down toward the hour.
'Werden' means to get or become for changing states: here 'wird es ... dunkel' = it gets dark.
'Hin' marks motion away from the speaker: 'zur Schule hin' = off to school. 'Her' would point back toward you.
Use 'nach' for cities and most countries meaning to: 'nach Hamburg' = to Hamburg, with no article.
Verbs like 'vergessen' add a 'zu'-infinitive set off by a comma: 'Ich habe vergessen, die Milch im Supermarkt zu kaufen'.
For exercise German normally uses 'Sport treiben' rather than 'Sport machen': here 'Sport zu treiben' = to do sports.
'Möchte' is the polite would like, softer than the blunt 'will' (want): 'möchte eine Tasse Tee' is a courteous way to order.
'Teilnehmen' fixes its object with 'an' plus the dative: 'an dem Fotografie-Workshop teilnehmen' = take part in the photography workshop.
With 'halb', German counts toward the coming hour: 'halb sieben' = 6:30, not 7:30.
'Ihm wurde ... geschenkt' is literally to him was gifted. German keeps the receiver in dative, 'ihm', where English promotes it to he was given.
'Weil' sends its verb to the very end: 'weil die Sonne blendet' puts 'blendet' last.
'Sich bedanken' uses 'bei' for the person and 'für' for the thing: 'bei Ihnen für die Gastfreundschaft'.
